historical_record.description: The Sharon Building went up at 300 Bowling Green Drive as a canteen for women and children, and is now a community art centre. One of the few Richardsonian Romanesque buildings in the city and the only local example with rough-hewn stone walls, it is City Landmark No. 124.
Designated San Francisco Landmark No. 124, Sharon Building.

Built to designs by Percy & Hamilton, with money William Sharon, the Comstock financier, left to the city, as the children's house and restaurant of the park's children's playground — with the carousel, the first public children's playground west of the Mississippi. It is a rare Victorian Romanesque building in sandstone; after 1906 it was rebuilt without its slate and copper roof.

On the Landmarks Preservation Advisory Board's recommendation, the City Planning Commission proposed, 4-1, that the Board of Supervisors designate the Sharon Building in Golden Gate Park a city landmark (Resolution 8752).
The Recreation and Park Commission approved the appointment of Norman C. Hall and Walter M. Sontheimer, architects, to prepare plans for repairing fire damage to the Sharon Building, for $7,800.
The Commission's Parks and Planning Committee reviewed and approved the preliminary plans for an Arts and Crafts Center in the Sharon Building.
The Recreation and Park Commission appointed Architectural Resources Group, for $15,000, to work on the Sharon Building's sandstone walls.

The Recreation and Park Commission gave conceptual approval to the third phase of the Sharon Building's restoration, drawn by the Bureau of Architecture, which put the exterior first: cleaning, replacing and waterproofing the sandstone, with new wood doors, metal gates and window grilles at the lower level.
The Recreation and Park Commission awarded Alpha Waterproofing & Restoration a $357,350 contract for Phase 3 of the Sharon Building restoration.
William Sharon's $50,000 bequest, first meant for a monumental gateway, was turned on the consulting engineer's advice to a children's house and playground.
Plans for the children's house were chosen from three submitted in competition by architectural firms; bids to build it were due on May 21, 1887.
Finished, and known at first as the Dairy, for the milk, bread and butter it was to serve to children; no cows were kept.
